objectives: Read the HR diagram + spectral classification.
Trace stellar nucleosynthesis from pp + CNO chains through r/s process.
Follow stellar lifecycle by initial mass.

slides.title: HR diagram + spectral classification
slides.body:
**Hertzsprung-Russell diagram**: the single most important plot in stellar astronomy. **Ejnar Hertzsprung (1911, Potsdam)** + independently **Henry Norris Russell (1913, Princeton)** plotted stars in (luminosity, temperature) — or equivalent (absolute magnitude, color) — space. They didn't fill the diagram uniformly; stars **cluster** into bands.

**Four main regions**:
1. **Main sequence (MS)**: diagonal band from top-left (hot, luminous, massive O stars, T~30000 K, L~10⁵ L☉) to bottom-right (cool, dim, low-mass M dwarfs, T~3000 K, L~10⁻³ L☉). **~90% of stars at any moment** — they're core H-fusing. The MS is *not* an evolutionary track; each star sits at one spot for most of its life.
2. **Red giants (RGB) + asymptotic giants (AGB)**: cool (3000-5000 K), luminous (10² - 10³ L☉) — upper-right. Post-MS, shell-H or He burning. Aldebaran, Arcturus.
3. **Supergiants**: extremely cool + extremely luminous (10⁴ - 10⁶ L☉) — top-right. Massive stars near death. Betelgeuse, Antares, Rigel (blue supergiant).
4. **White dwarfs**: hot (8000-100000 K) but very faint (10⁻² - 10⁻⁴ L☉) — bottom-left. Earth-sized degenerate stellar corpses.

**Spectral classification — OBAFGKM** ('Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy Kiss Me'):
Established by **Annie Jump Cannon** + Pickering at Harvard (1890-1924) by re-ordering the original Secchi/Pickering letter sequence into a **temperature sequence** of ~250000 stars (the *Henry Draper Catalogue*):
- **O** (>30000 K, blue): He II + N III + Si IV lines; rare massive stars; OB associations.
- **B** (10000-30000 K, blue-white): He I + H Balmer; Rigel, Spica.
- **A** (7500-10000 K, white): strong H Balmer; Vega, Sirius A.
- **F** (6000-7500 K, yellow-white): H + metals; Procyon, Polaris.
- **G** (5200-6000 K, yellow): metal lines + Ca H + K; **Sun** (G2V).
- **K** (3700-5200 K, orange): TiO bands appearing; Arcturus, Aldebaran.
- **M** (<3700 K, red): TiO + VO dominant; Proxima Centauri, Betelgeuse (M-supergiant).

**Morgan-Keenan luminosity classes** (Morgan + Keenan + Kellman 1943, *MKK Atlas*): adds the **second dimension** to spectral type, encoding luminosity (gravity-sensitive line widths):
- **I**: supergiants (Ia bright + Ib normal).
- **II**: bright giants.
- **III**: giants.
- **IV**: subgiants.
- **V**: main sequence (dwarfs).
- **VI / sd**: subdwarfs (metal-poor).
- **VII / D**: white dwarfs.

The Sun = **G2V** (mid-G, main sequence). Sirius A = A1V. Betelgeuse = M2Iab (cool supergiant). Modern surveys add finer classifications (L, T, Y for brown dwarfs + ultracool objects).

**Mass is the master parameter**: nearly everything about a star — luminosity, radius, temperature, lifetime, fate — is determined primarily by its initial mass + (to second order) metallicity. The HR diagram is a snapshot — what you see is the **age-distribution-weighted superposition** of all currently-burning stars.

slides.title: Stellar nucleosynthesis: how stars build the periodic table
slides.body:
Stars are **nuclear furnaces** + **factories of the periodic table**. Hydrogen + helium were forged in BBN; everything else comes from stars.

**Bethe (1939)**: identified the two H-burning chains that power main-sequence stars:

**pp chain** (proton-proton): dominant in stars M ≲ 1.3 M☉ (Sun + cooler).
- pp I: 4 ¹H → ⁴He + 2 e⁺ + 2 ν_e + γ + 26.7 MeV per cycle (matter → energy via E = mc²).
- Rate ∝ T⁴ (steeply temperature-dependent, but less than CNO).
- Solar core: T ≈ 15.7 MK; ρ ≈ 150 g/cm³.

**CNO cycle** (Bethe 1939; Carbon-Nitrogen-Oxygen catalytic): dominant in massive stars (>1.3 M☉) where T > 17 MK.
- ¹²C + ¹H → ... → ⁴He + ¹²C; C/N/O isotopes act as catalysts.
- Rate ∝ T¹⁵-¹⁸ — extremely T-sensitive → very steep T gradient → convective core in massive stars.
- Net same: 4 H → He + energy.

Both produce **solar neutrinos** — detected by Davis (Homestake chlorine, 1968) + Kamiokande + SNO. **Pontecorvo + Bahcall**'s solar-neutrino problem (1968-2002, missing ⅔ of predicted ν_e) was resolved by neutrino oscillation discovery (McDonald + Kajita Nobel 2015) — vindicated standard solar model.

**Post-MS nucleosynthesis** — Margaret + Geoffrey Burbidge + William Fowler + Fred Hoyle (**B²FH paper**, 1957 RMP) systematically catalogued how stars build all heavier elements. Fowler Nobel 1983; cited as foundational of stellar nucleosynthesis.

**Helium burning** (T ~ 100 MK):
- **Triple-alpha process**: 3 ⁴He → ¹²C via ⁸Be intermediate (Hoyle 1953 predicted resonance to explain ¹²C abundance — confirmed; classic example of anthropic resonance).
- ¹²C + α → ¹⁶O (also abundant).
- Burns in core after MS turnoff → He-burning red-giants + horizontal-branch stars.

**Advanced burning** (massive stars, T = 0.5-3 GK):
- C-burning → Ne + Na + Mg.
- Ne-burning → O + Mg.
- O-burning → Si + S + Ar + Ca.
- Si-burning → Fe-group (iron peak: ⁵⁶Fe most stable nucleus per nucleon).
- **Iron core** + further fusion is **endothermic** (no more energy from fusing past Fe) → core collapse → supernova.

Onion-shell structure: H envelope outside He shell outside C shell outside ... Fe core.

**Neutron-capture nucleosynthesis** (B²FH 1957) builds elements heavier than iron (no fusion past Fe; need neutron capture):
- **s-process** (slow): neutron capture slower than β-decay; runs along valley of stability through Sr, Ba, Pb. Occurs in AGB stars + massive-star He shells.
- **r-process** (rapid): neutron capture much faster than β-decay; builds neutron-rich exotic isotopes then decays; produces ~half of elements heavier than Fe + all transuranic + actinides (Au, Pt, U, Th). **Sites**: long debated; **GW170817 kilonova** (2017 NS-NS merger, multi-messenger) confirmed compact-object mergers as primary r-process site — gold + platinum literally forged in cosmic NS collisions.
- **p-process** (proton-rich isotopes): rare; supernova shocks.

**Cosmic abundances**: H 75% + He 24% (mostly BBN); C/N/O/Ne 1%; Fe-peak + heavier elements <0.1% (all from stars). 'We are stardust' (Carl Sagan, Joni Mitchell, B²FH) is literal — every atom heavier than He in your body was synthesized in a star or stellar explosion.

slides.title: Stellar lifecycle: birth, life, death by mass
slides.body:
A star's entire evolution is set primarily by its **initial mass**. Below is the standard sequence:

**Star formation — birth**:
- **Molecular cloud collapse**: cold (~10 K), dense (~10² - 10⁴ cm⁻³) regions of GMCs (e.g. Orion, Taurus, Eagle Nebula 'Pillars of Creation'). Triggered by turbulence + shocks + magnetic instabilities + Jeans instability when gravity overcomes thermal + magnetic + turbulent support.
- **Protostar phase**: collapsing cloud heats; surrounded by **circumstellar disk** + bipolar outflows. Class 0/I/II/III phases (Lada + Wilking 1984). Observable in IR + sub-mm (Spitzer, ALMA).
- **T Tauri stars** (low-mass pre-MS): contracting, accreting from disk, visible in optical + IR + X-ray. ~1-10 Myr to reach MS.
- **Herbig Ae/Be stars**: intermediate-mass equivalents.
- **O stars**: massive pre-MS contraction is so fast they reach MS while still embedded in their natal cloud (~10⁵ yr).

Initial Mass Function (IMF; **Salpeter 1955**): dN/dM ∝ M^(-2.35) for M > 0.5 M☉. Most stars are low-mass (M dwarfs ~75%); massive stars are rare but luminous + short-lived.

**Main sequence — life**: H-burning in core. Position + lifetime depend on mass:
- L ∝ M^3.5, t_MS ∝ M / L ∝ M^(-2.5).
- 100 M☉ O star: ~3 Myr.
- 10 M☉ B star: ~30 Myr.
- 1 M☉ Sun: 10 Gyr.
- 0.5 M☉ M dwarf: ~50-200 Gyr (longer than age of universe).
- 0.1 M☉ M dwarf: ~Tyr.

**Eddington limit**: maximum luminosity where radiation pressure outward equals gravitational pull inward. L_Edd ≈ 3.2×10⁴ L☉ × (M/M☉). Above L_Edd, star drives massive winds — limits maximum stellar mass to ~150 M☉ (sets via instability). Most massive known: R136a1 (~200-300 M☉; Tarantula Nebula).

**Post-main-sequence — death by mass**:
- **M < 0.5 M☉**: never ignites He core. Eventually becomes **He white dwarf** (universe isn't old enough yet — projected fate).
- **0.5 ≲ M < 8 M☉** (Sun): leaves MS → **red giant branch** (RGB; H-shell burning, core contracting) → **He flash** (degenerate core ignites runaway He burning) → **horizontal branch** (core He burning) → **asymptotic giant branch** (AGB; He + H shells; thermal pulses + mass loss via stellar winds) → **planetary nebula** (Hubble's misnomer — looks planet-like in small scopes; really expanding shell of ionized gas: Ring, Helix, Cat's Eye, Eskimo) → **carbon-oxygen white dwarf** (~0.6 M☉; Earth-sized; held up by electron degeneracy; cools eternally to black dwarf).
- **8 ≲ M < 25 M☉**: blue + red supergiant → onion-shell burning → iron core → **core-collapse supernova (Type II / Ib / Ic)** → **neutron star** (~1.4-2.2 M☉; ~10 km radius; nuclear density; pulsars Bell + Hewish 1967). NS supported by neutron degeneracy.
- **25 ≲ M ≲ 100 M☉**: similar but more mass loss + larger Fe core → core-collapse SN → **stellar-mass black hole** (a few - 30 M☉). LIGO BBH mergers (since GW150914 2015) revealed populations of ~30 M☉ BHs not seen before electromagnetically.
- **M > ~140 M☉**: **pair-instability supernova** — γ-ray photons produce e⁻e⁺ pairs in core, reducing pressure support → catastrophic collapse + total disruption (no remnant). Rare; some Population III + low-metallicity stars likely went this route.

**Chandrasekhar limit (1931, Nobel 1983)**: maximum mass of a white dwarf supportable by electron degeneracy ≈ **1.4 M☉**. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar derived this as a 19-year-old on the boat from India to Cambridge; opposed publicly by Eddington (who insisted nature would 'protect' against this). Above 1.4 M☉ → degenerate pressure can't hold → collapse to NS or BH.

**Type Ia supernova**: a CO white dwarf in a binary either accretes mass + crosses Chandrasekhar limit → thermonuclear runaway (single-degenerate channel), or two WDs merge (double-degenerate). Total disruption + characteristic light curve. **Standardizable candles** (Phillips relation) → Perlmutter + Schmidt + Riess 1998 → accelerating expansion → dark energy → 2011 Nobel.

**Type II supernova**: massive star core collapse. Light curve dominated by H envelope + ⁵⁶Ni decay; produces NS or BH. Sn1987A in LMC is closest modern example — Kamiokande + IMB + Baksan detected the **neutrino burst** ~3 hr before optical brightening, confirming core-collapse model.

**Stellar evolution + nucleosynthesis** turn the universe from a hot H + He soup into the chemically diverse cosmos we observe. We are made of stardust.

question.question: Estimate the Sun's main-sequence lifetime from first principles
question.goal: Use mass-energy + nuclear-physics + luminosity to estimate t_MS for the Sun. Compare to detailed model (~10 Gyr).

steps.prompt: Energy per H→He fusion: 0.7% of rest mass via E=mc². How much energy in one solar mass of H if all converted?
steps.reveal: ΔE = 0.007 × M☉ × c² = 0.007 × 2×10³⁰ × 9×10¹⁶ ≈ 1.26×10⁴⁵ J (total chemical → nuclear conversion efficiency 0.7%). Most efficient process in the universe outside accretion onto BH.

steps.prompt: Only ~10% of solar mass (core, > ~7% of mass) is hot enough to fuse. Available energy?
steps.reveal: E_avail ≈ 0.1 × 1.26×10⁴⁵ ≈ 1.26×10⁴⁴ J. Only core H gets hot + dense enough for fusion; envelope H is never consumed.

steps.prompt: Lifetime t = E / L. Solar luminosity L☉ = 3.83×10²⁶ W. Compute.
steps.reveal: t = E/L = 1.26×10⁴⁴ / 3.83×10²⁶ ≈ 3.3×10¹⁷ s ≈ 10.4 Gyr. Remarkable agreement with detailed stellar-evolution models (~10 Gyr for the Sun). Sun is ~4.6 Gyr old; ~5 Gyr remain on MS.

steps.prompt: Why does t_MS scale as M^(-2.5) instead of just M?
steps.motivation: Fuel ∝ M but burn rate ∝ L ∝ M^3.5.

acceptedAnswers: t ∝ M/L ∝ M / M^3.5 = M^(-2.5) — more massive stars have more fuel but burn it disproportionately faster

steps.reveal: Total fuel scales as M (more mass = more H to burn). But luminosity (burn rate) scales much more steeply: L ∝ M^3.5 (Eddington's mass-luminosity relation, ~confirmed observationally). So lifetime t ∝ M/L ∝ M^(-2.5). 10× more massive star burns ~3000× faster but only has 10× more fuel → lives ~316× shorter. This is why O stars are rare + short-lived + always in star-forming regions, while M dwarfs effectively immortal.

question.question: Why was the Chandrasekhar limit (1.4 M☉) so consequential for stellar end states?
options: Chandrasekhar (1931, Nobel 1983) showed that electron degeneracy pressure has a maximum supportable mass ≈ 1.4 M☉ for cold non-rotating WD. Above this, gravitational collapse cannot be halted by electrons → must collapse further to NS (held by neutron degeneracy, ~2 M☉ limit Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff) or BH (above TOV limit). The limit also enables Type Ia supernovae (WD accreting past Chandrasekhar → thermonuclear runaway → standardizable candle → Perlmutter/Schmidt/Riess 1998 → dark energy → 2011 Nobel). Single equation that determines whether a stellar corpse becomes WD, NS, or BH.
question.explanation: Chandrasekhar (1931, Nobel 1983) derived M_Ch = 1.4 M☉ as the maximum mass an electron-degenerate WD can support. Above this: catastrophic collapse → NS (TOV limit ~2-2.5 M☉) or BH (above TOV). The 1.4 M☉ value is also the trigger for Type Ia SNe (accreting WD crosses limit → thermonuclear runaway → standard candle → dark-energy discovery). One physical constant that sets WD/NS/BH boundaries + enabled cosmological-acceleration discovery.

hints: What determines the end state of a star?
How does it relate to Type Ia SNe?
slides.workedSolution: Chandrasekhar (1931, Nobel 1983): M_Ch ≈ 1.4 M☉ is the maximum mass of an electron-degenerate WD. Below = stable WD; above = collapse to NS or BH (TOV ~2-2.5 M☉ for neutron-degenerate NS). Type Ia SNe = WDs accreting across M_Ch → thermonuclear explosion → standardizable candles → 1998 dark-energy discovery. Eddington famously opposed the result; Chandrasekhar derived it as a 19-yr-old.

question.question: The neutron-star merger event GW170817 (Aug 17, 2017) was the first multi-messenger detection of a binary NS merger — gravitational waves + gamma-ray burst + optical/IR kilonova + radio afterglow.
question.prompt: Walk through what stellar-evolution + nucleosynthesis implications it confirmed: (1) two NSs formed from progenitor massive stars; (2) gravitational radiation drove them to merge after ~Gyr; (3) the kilonova (~2-3 days post-merger, faded over weeks) showed UV/optical/IR spectral evolution consistent with r-process nucleosynthesis — Pian + Tanvir + Smartt + Drout 2017 papers identified Au + Pt + Sr + Te + lanthanide signatures; (4) this confirms compact-object mergers as a primary site of r-process — solving a 60-year B²FH problem (Burbidge × 2 + Fowler + Hoyle 1957). What were the alternative sites (core-collapse SNe, magnetars)? What does Cosmic Explorer + LISA promise for future multimessenger r-process science?

question.question: Write the main-sequence lifetime scaling with mass (in solar units).
question.hint: Combine fuel (∝ M) with burn rate (L ∝ M^3.5).

slides.workedSolution: t_MS ≈ 10 Gyr × (M/M☉)^(-2.5). Sun (M=1): 10 Gyr. 10 M☉: 32 Myr. 50 M☉: ~600 kyr. 0.5 M☉: ~57 Gyr. 0.1 M☉: ~Tyr. Strong dependence on mass — drives the structure of HR diagram + globular-cluster turnoff ages + IMF-weighted galactic evolution.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how stellar physics built every atom heavier than helium in your body.
question.rubric: Mentions: BBN produced only H + He + traces of Li (no C, N, O, Fe, etc.). Stars: pp + CNO chains (Bethe 1939) fuse H→He on MS. Post-MS: triple-α (Hoyle 1953 resonance) makes ¹²C; α-capture → ¹⁶O. Advanced burning in massive stars: C → Ne, Ne → O, O → Si, Si → Fe-peak. Iron most stable; further fusion endothermic → core collapse. Beyond Fe: neutron capture (B²FH 1957 — Burbidge × 2 + Fowler + Hoyle): s-process in AGB (slow capture, Sr, Ba, Pb) + r-process in NS-NS mergers (rapid capture; GW170817 confirmed Au, Pt, lanthanides). Supernovae + stellar winds disperse newly-forged elements to ISM → next-generation stars + planets. Every atom heavier than He in your body — C in proteins, O in water, Fe in hemoglobin, I in thyroid, Au in jewelry — was forged in a star or stellar explosion + then recycled. 'We are stardust' (Carl Sagan).
